jobsToBeDone.name: Launch a new energy proposition in weeks, not months
jobsToBeDone.whatItIs: Take a proposition from an idea in the commercial team to a live product customers can buy: define the contract type, tariff structure and commercial rules, configure the product and pricing logic, design the sign-up journey and channel availability, test the whole chain from order to first invoice on real market flows, and release it with monitoring in place. Applies equally to a fixed one-year contract, a dynamic 15-minute tariff, an EV night tariff or a bundled solar-and-battery proposition.
jobsToBeDone.outcome: The proposition is live within weeks on the channels chosen, every contract created from it flows through switching, meter data and billing without custom code, and the first invoices and the campaign funnel confirm that the product behaves as designed.

customerJourneyStories.name: From an eighteen-month IT queue to a proposition studio
customerJourneyStories.summary: A proposition manager at a green Dutch supplier with 300,000 connections lives through the move from a heritage billing engine, where every tariff change was a development ticket, to a low-code proposition builder plugged into the order-to-cash backbone, from the dynamic EV tariff that a competitor launched first to the quarter in which the team ships three propositions itself.

stages.narrative: The supplier's dynamic EV night tariff has been in the IT backlog for fourteen months when a competitor launches one on the comparison sites and the 15-minute day-ahead market of September 2025 makes the specification obsolete again. The commercial director tells the proposition manager that eighteen months to launch a product is eighteen months for competitors to land first, and asks for a way to launch without waiting for the billing release train.

At an industry event the proposition manager hears a peer from Pure Energie describe configuring a proposition in weeks on the platform their supplier already uses for market communication and billing, and reads the vendor's Dutch market review on Allocation 2.0 and the 15-minute market. A demo of the proposition builder shows a tariff, journey and campaign configured and flowing into a contract and an invoice in one session.

The proposition manager, the billing manager and IT compare extending the heritage billing engine with a configuration layer against the platform's Supplier Suite with the proposition studio. Decisive checks are whether dynamic and time-of-use tariffs settle on the same 15-minute prices the portfolio desk sources on, whether energy tax, VAT, grid fees and the ACM disclosures are modeled rather than scripted, how comparison-site connectors work, and what migrating contracts and tariffs from the old engine costs. A reference call with a supplier already live on the builder settles the risk question.

One proposition goes first: the EV night tariff is configured in the sandbox in three weeks, run through switching, meter data and billing with test connections, and launched on the supplier's own web shop only. The first two hundred contracts switch and receive advances without a manual correction, and the first monthly invoices show the night and day blocks exactly as the business case priced them.

The commercial team takes over configuration entirely: a solar-return proposition, a fixed two-year contract for the winter campaign and a home-battery tariff follow within a quarter, campaigns are switched on and off per comparison site from the campaign module, and realised margin per proposition appears next to the sourcing cost every week. Tariff changes for variable contracts are published with their notices from the same product version.

At renewal the proposition manager presents three propositions launched per quarter instead of one per year, a campaign conversion rate above plan and no billing corrections traced to configuration. The supplier extends the subscription with the campaign and comparison-site connectors, sends two commercial colleagues to the academy, and the manager speaks at the vendor's customer day about launching in weeks.

customerJourneyStories.name: An Iberian supplier reprices sixty thousand contracts on one platform
customerJourneyStories.summary: A product and pricing lead at a Catalan comercializadora with 60,000 supply points moves from spreadsheets and a custom CRM to Nemon Trade Energy and, after the acquisition, to the group's proposition and pricing tooling, from a regulated tariff change that had to be applied overnight to a portfolio priced on OMIE curves with the margin visible per segment.

stages.narrative: A CNMC change to the access tariffs and a jump in OMIE prices force the supplier to reprice every indexed and fixed contract within weeks. The pricing lead rebuilds the price tables in spreadsheets, the CRM developer patches the invoicing script over a weekend, and a few thousand invoices go out with the old time-period prices. The managing director asks for pricing that lives in the system rather than in a spreadsheet.

The pricing lead learns from Barcelona Energia and other suppliers in the regional energy association that around a hundred Iberian suppliers run their commercial operation on Nemon's Trade Energy suite, and after the 2026 acquisition by Eneve sees at a user meeting how the group's proposition and pricing tooling is coming to the Iberian platform: versioned tariffs, OMIE-indexed pricing logic, PVPC and social-bonus rules and margin tracking per segment.

The pricing lead compares staying on the custom CRM with a pricing module bolted on, another Spanish supplier platform, and the Iberian supplier platform of the group. The checks that matter are SIPS and ATR switching with the distributors, 2.0TD and 3.0TD time-period tariffs with electricity tax and VAT, indexation to OMIE day-ahead with pass-through of adjustment costs, CNMC reporting, Catalan and Spanish customer documents, and the promise that Dutch-style proposition configuration arrives on the same platform without a migration.

The supplier moves its indexed B2B portfolio first: contracts, CUPS and price formulas are migrated, one billing cycle runs in parallel with the old CRM, and the first OMIE-indexed invoices match the spreadsheet to the cent. A new fixed-price household product is configured as a versioned tariff with its regulatory disclosures and sold through the web shop within a month.

The pricing lead maintains price curves and cost-plus mark-ups in the platform, versions tariffs with effective dates, and sees realised margin per segment against the sourcing cost every week. Tariff changes for indexed contracts are published with their notices from the product version, and the supplier launches a solar self-consumption proposition and a small-business time-of-use product in the same quarter.

At the first renewal after the acquisition, the supplier has repriced its portfolio twice without a manual invoice correction, launched four products in a year and cut the pricing spreadsheet out of the operation. It takes the campaign module and the group's margin analytics, and the pricing lead versions the tariffs for the new Portuguese book on the same product catalogue.

customerJourneyStories.name: From a heritage billing engine and a switching team to straight-through order-to-cash
customerJourneyStories.summary: A billing and operations manager at a Dutch supplier with 450,000 connections lives through the move from a customised billing engine, a separate market-communication tool and a switching team working from mailboxes to one order-to-cash backbone, from the Allocation 2.0 deadline that the old vendor could not meet to the renewal in which the supplier asks for AI-assisted exception triage.

stages.narrative: Allocation 2.0 tranche 3 requires reconciliation via the TenneT MMC-Hub from 1 January 2025 and the old billing vendor quotes a nine-month custom project, while the exception queue after the winter annual settlements stands at 12,000 invoices and the switching team works rejections from a shared mailbox. The COO tells the operations manager that market changes must come from the vendor and that the next annual settlement round must not need a temp team.

The operations manager knows the vendor's market-communication platform from the BRP desk, which already receives its allocation data through it, and learns at the Dutch supplier association that suppliers such as Vandebron and Mega run intake, billing and customer care on the same platform. A visit to a supplier's back office shows the exception queue worked by cause and the Allocation 2.0 change already in production across tenants.

The supplier compares upgrading the heritage engine with an added market-communication module against the Supplier Suite. The decisive checks are that EDSN, C-AR and MMC-Hub changes are delivered by the vendor before market dates, the billing engine's pre-run check and exception routing, split invoicing and guarantees of origin for the B2B portfolio, direct-debit and dunning with disconnection prevention, ERP connectors, and a migration plan for 450,000 connections with contract history and readings. The vendor's track record of validating most of the Dutch consumption data and the security and continuity documentation satisfy the CFO and the auditor.

The B2B portfolio of 25,000 connections migrates first with the vendor's migration tooling, one billing cycle runs in parallel with the old engine, and the switching team works one month of B2B intake from the rejection queue. Billed volumes reconcile with allocated volumes within tolerance, the parallel run matches the old invoices except for the errors the old engine had been making, and the queue for the B2B set is cleared by cause in days.

The household portfolio moves over before the next annual settlement round. Intake runs straight through from every channel, the pre-run check holds a few hundred invoices per cycle instead of thousands, corrections re-invoice without ledger work, direct debits and dunning run on schedule, and the period closes with the volume and cash reconciliations in the close pack. The 15-minute day-ahead change of September 2025 arrives as a vendor release tested on the tenant before the market date.

At renewal the operations manager shows a straight-through billing rate in the high nineties, annual settlements all within the regulatory term, no temp team and a lower cost to serve per connection. The supplier adds the open API for its ERP and data warehouse, asks the vendor about AI-assisted exception triage, and the operations manager joins the vendor's customer advisory group on market communication.

customerJourneyStories.name: An Iberian comercializadora ends the distributor-file scramble
customerJourneyStories.summary: An operations manager at a Spanish supplier with 90,000 supply points moves switching, billing and collections from a custom CRM and manual ATR file handling with five distributors to the Iberian supplier platform, from a CNMC billing-timeliness warning to a monthly close that reconciles supply points, volumes and cash without spreadsheets.

stages.narrative: Switching files exchanged with five distributors are rejected in batches because of format changes, monthly invoices for indexed customers go out late once the OMIE prices and adjustment costs are entered by hand, and CNMC sends a warning on billing timeliness. The operations manager spends the close reconciling supply points between the CRM, the distributor files and the accounting package.

At a supplier association meeting the operations manager hears that Barcelona Energia and dozens of other Iberian suppliers run switching, billing and collections on Nemon Trade Energy, and that the suite now belongs to a European group that maintains market communication for the Dutch market as well. A demo shows ATR and SIPS handling as automated processes with a rejection worklist and indexed billing running on OMIE prices pulled in automatically.

The supplier compares patching the custom CRM, another Spanish supplier system and the Iberian supplier platform. The checks that count are automated ATR switching and SIPS lookups for every distributor, 2.0TD and 3.0TD invoicing with electricity tax, VAT and the social bonus, OMIE-indexed billing with adjustment costs, SEPA direct debit and dunning under the Spanish disconnection rules, CNMC reporting, an accounting connector, and a migration of 90,000 supply points with history. References from two suppliers of similar size close the decision.

The business portfolio of 8,000 supply points migrates first, one monthly cycle runs in parallel, and the switching team works a month of ATR requests from the platform's rejection queue instead of the distributor portals. Invoices match the old system, rejections drop once the distributor format rules are applied automatically, and the month's close for the business set takes two days.

The household portfolio follows within the quarter. Switching runs straight through with every distributor, monthly indexed and fixed-price invoices go out on schedule with the regulated components applied, direct debits and dunning run from the platform, and the operations manager closes the month with supply points, volumes and cash reconciled on one report. Regulatory format changes arrive as vendor releases tested before the effective date.

At renewal the supplier shows CNMC-compliant billing timeliness, a correction rate a fraction of the old one, and a back office that did not grow while the portfolio did. It takes the white-label portal and the group's dashboards, and the operations manager's next project is moving the gas portfolio onto the same monthly close.

customerJourneyStories.name: From a bolt-on portal that disagreed with the invoice to self-service on the backbone
customerJourneyStories.summary: A customer service lead at a Dutch supplier with 600,000 customers moves from a separately built portal fed by nightly exports, a contact-centre CRM without billing context and a mailing tool, to the white-label portal, case management and communication on the operational backbone, from the price-crisis winter that tripled calls to the renewal in which self-service resolves three quarters of needs.

stages.narrative: During the winter after the 2022 price shock, advances and annual settlements change for every customer, the portal built on nightly exports shows balances that differ from the invoice, and calls triple while agents toggle between the CRM, the billing screens and the meter-data tool. Complaints reach the dispute committee and the regulator asks about tariff-change notices. The board asks the service lead for a channel customers can trust and a contact centre that can see what billing sees.

The service lead learns from the billing manager that the supplier's billing platform vendor offers a white-label portal and case management on the same data, and hears at a customer-experience network that suppliers such as Vandebron and Mega run their customer channels this way. A demo shows an invoice breakdown, 15-minute consumption and a tariff-change notice in the portal drawn live from the billing records, and a case opened with the full context.

The supplier compares rebuilding its own portal on a customer-experience platform against the vendor's white-label portal, app and care modules. The checks that count are that portal data is the billing data rather than a copy, self-service requests execute as operational processes, multi-brand isolation for the supplier's two labels, app-store presence, accessibility and security review, regulatory document generation for ACM disclosures, contact-centre integration and the migration of customer accounts and consent. Peer references and a look at the vendor's release cadence for market changes settle it.

The smaller label goes first: its 80,000 customers get the new portal and app, invoices and consumption appear from the backbone, meter readings and advance changes execute in the operation, and agents handle that label's contacts in the new case desk. Within two months the label's contact rate drops and the difference between portal and invoice disappears from the complaint causes.

The main label follows before the next annual settlement round. Customers read their settlement with a breakdown and consumption in the app, tariff-change notices and contract-end offers are generated from the contract data, agents diagnose bill questions from readings and tariff history in the case, and root causes flow to billing and the proposition team. Churn-risk flags drive renewal offers in the portal before the comparison-site season.

At renewal the service lead reports self-service resolution up by a third, contact rate per connection down, dispute cases within term and a higher satisfaction score. The supplier adds the communication module for its business segment and asks the vendor for AI-assisted case resolution before the next switching season.

customerJourneyStories.name: A municipal Iberian supplier gives its customers a portal in two languages
customerJourneyStories.summary: A customer service lead at a public supplier in Catalonia with 45,000 customers moves from e-mail forms and a phone line to the white-label portal and communication on the Iberian supplier platform, from a social-bonus and PVPC communication scramble to lifecycle communication in Catalan and Spanish generated from the contract data.

stages.narrative: A regulated tariff change and a social-bonus renewal round hit at once, the team mails 45,000 notices by hand from a spreadsheet, customers cannot see their consumption or invoices online, and the municipality's complaints office receives letters about bills nobody can explain quickly. The director asks the service lead for a digital channel and communication that come from the system the invoices come from.

The service lead sees at a Nemon user meeting how other Iberian suppliers give customers a portal on the Trade Energy platform and learns that the group behind it runs white-label portals for millions of Dutch households. A demo shows invoices, consumption, meter readings and service requests in Catalan and Spanish, with social-bonus and PVPC notices generated per customer.

The supplier compares a portal from a web agency fed by exports with the platform's white-label portal and communication module. The checks that decide are that the portal reads the billing and CUPS data directly, bilingual content and documents, social-bonus and regulated-tariff disclosures generated per customer, accessibility for a public body, data protection review, contact-centre case management and the cost for a small team. References from two suppliers of similar size and the public-procurement documentation settle it.

The portal launches for the business customers and the municipality's own buildings first, showing invoices with the regulated components and interval consumption, and service requests flow into the case desk. Within six weeks the team sends its first tariff-change notice to that segment from the platform in both languages with delivery evidence.

Households follow with an activation campaign on the invoice. Customers submit readings, change payment details and download documents themselves, the social-bonus renewal round runs as generated communication with a case for each response, agents resolve bill questions from the case with readings and tariff history, and contact causes feed back to billing and pricing.

At renewal the service lead shows a contact rate half of what it was, notices sent on time for every regulated change and complaint letters to the municipality down to a handful. The supplier adds the mobile app and asks for churn-risk flags ahead of the next market-price cycle, and the service lead gives the municipality's social-services office its own case-desk access so payment-difficulty cases are handled together.

customers.name: Portfolio and Trading Manager
customers.description: Sources and hedges the electricity and gas portfolio of a supplier or trading company, maintains the price curves and the cost-plus pricing that every proposition and B2B quote is built on, and watches positions, volumes, value and risk per customer segment. Typical employer: the portfolio desk of a Dutch supplier such as Pure Energie, Vattenfall or PZEM, or the Benelux origination and portfolio team of an international BRP such as Axpo or TotalEnergies, running a portfolio of a few hundred GWh to several TWh a year with a desk of three to ten traders and analysts. Since the day-ahead market moved to 15-minute blocks on 30 September 2025 the desk values its position 96 times a day instead of 24, and every retail proposition, every producer PPA and every industrial click contract changes that position.
careAbout: A hedging strategy that is executed as planned: forward, day-ahead and PPA volumes covering the forecast demand of each segment within the agreed open-position limits, with the coverage visible per delivery period

One price curve set — forward curves, EPEX 15-minute day-ahead, TTF gas, guarantees of origin, imbalance and profile costs — that feeds cost-plus pricing so that retail tariffs, B2B quotes and click contracts are priced from the same numbers the portfolio is valued on

Positions, volumes and value per segment (residential fixed, variable, dynamic, B2B multi-site, producers, flex assets) updated every 15 minutes from allocation and forecast data rather than from a weekly spreadsheet
Risk exposures (volume risk from churn and weather, price risk on open positions, profile and imbalance cost) spotted before they hit the margin, with an action attached to every deviation
B2B deals priced from the actual portfolio position and profile cost, with a quote out in hours and the margin tracked after the deal closes
A sourcing cost and gross margin per MWh the CFO can reconcile to the settlement invoices and the billing runs
winsThem: Position tracking that combines allocated volumes from Allocation 2.0, portfolio forecasts and executed hedges per segment and per 15-minute block, so the open position is a number on a screen and not the result of a Monday-morning export
Price curves and cost-plus pricing maintained once and pushed to the proposition builder, the quoting tool and the customer trading desk, ending the drift between what was priced and what was sourced
Hedge transactions captured where they are executed and immediately reflected in coverage, value and risk, with limits that alert instead of being checked at month end
A 15-minute financial view per segment that shows where margin is made or lost, which the desk can share with the CFO and the proposition team without a translation layer
Deal structuring for B2B contracts (fixed, tranche, click, pass-through) that produces the quote, the risk reservation and the contract terms from the same profile and curve data
theirFear: A retail campaign that sells thousands of fixed contracts while the desk is under-hedged, so the portfolio buys the volume at a market price far above the tariff and the campaign becomes the year's biggest loss
A price curve updated in the pricing tool but not in the position valuation, so the desk reports a margin that the settlement invoice later contradicts
An industrial click contract executed by a customer at a price the desk had not hedged, discovered only when the position report shows an open volume for the whole delivery year

jobsToBeDone.name: Source and hedge the portfolio at the right cost and risk
jobsToBeDone.whatItIs: From the demand and production forecast per segment to a portfolio that is procured on forward, day-ahead and PPA markets according to a hedging strategy, with open positions kept inside risk limits and the sourcing cost reported against the margin the propositions were priced on.
jobsToBeDone.outcome: The portfolio is covered as the strategy prescribes for every delivery period, hedges are executed with little slippage, open positions stay within limits as customers come and go, and the sourcing cost per MWh is known and reconcilable at all times.

steps.step: Define the hedging strategy and open-position limits

jobsToBeDone.outcome: The desk, the proposition team and the CFO look at the same position, volume and value per segment, refreshed every 15 minutes, and every deviation from plan has an owner and an action before it becomes a settlement surprise.

steps.step: Define segments and attribute every contract to one
steps.description: Set up the segments the portfolio is steered on (residential fixed, variable, dynamic, EV and battery propositions, B2B multi-site, producers, flex assets) and the rules that attribute each supply contract, PPA and connection to a segment as propositions are launched or changed.

streamsNeeded.name: Source and Price the Portfolio
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Maintains the segment structure and the attribution rules that all positions and values are grouped by.

streamsNeeded.name: Launch Energy Propositions and Tariffs
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Tags every new proposition with its segment and pricing basis at launch so contracts land in the right position from the first sale.

steps.step: Get allocated and forecast volumes per segment per 15-minute block
steps.description: Pull the allocated volumes from Allocation 2.0, the validated telemetry of large connections and the portfolio forecast for periods not yet allocated, and aggregate them per segment and 15-minute block for the current day, the week and the delivery months ahead.

streamsNeeded.name: Settle, Allocate and Reconcile Market Volumes
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Delivers the allocated volumes per connection type and interval that make up the realised part of the position.

streamsNeeded.name: Collect and Validate Meter Data
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Provides near real-time telemetry of large and flexible connections for the intervals allocation has not yet covered.

streamsNeeded.name: Forecast and Nominate the Portfolio
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Fills the forward part of the position with the forecast per segment used for nominations.

steps.step: Value positions against the current price curves
steps.description: Value the hedged and open volumes per segment against the forward curves, the 15-minute day-ahead prices and the TTF gas curve, including profile, imbalance and guarantee-of-origin costs, so margin per segment is a number that updates with the market.

streamsNeeded.name: Source and Price the Portfolio
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Applies the maintained price curves and cost components to positions to produce value and margin per segment.

steps.step: Spot risks and deviations that need an action
steps.description: Compare the position against the hedging plan and the risk limits, and detect the deviations that matter: a segment growing faster than hedged, a producer PPA under-delivering, an intraday position drifting, a curve move that turns a segment's margin negative.

streamsNeeded.name: Source and Price the Portfolio
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Runs the limit and deviation checks and raises alerts with the segment, period and size of the exposure.

streamsNeeded.name: Steer Intraday and Optimise Imbalance
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Shows the intraday position and the expected imbalance so short-term deviations are visible next to the long-term ones.

steps.step: Take action: rebalance, re-price or steer
steps.description: Turn each deviation into an action: an additional hedge, a tariff or price-curve update for the proposition team, a request to the BRP desk to steer intraday, or a hold on a campaign, and record the decision against the position it addressed.

streamsNeeded.name: Source and Price the Portfolio
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Records the rebalancing trades and price-curve changes and shows their effect on coverage and margin.

streamsNeeded.name: Steer Intraday and Optimise Imbalance
streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Hands the short-term part of the action to the intraday steering cycle so ETPA trades or flex steering close the gap.

customerJourneyStories.name: Moving the portfolio desk off spreadsheets after the 15-minute day-ahead change
customerJourneyStories.summary: The portfolio manager of a mid-sized Dutch supplier with a growing dynamic-tariff and producer book adopts the Trade and Portfolio Suite when the 15-minute day-ahead market and Allocation 2.0 make the desk's spreadsheet positions unworkable, and ends up with a 15-minute view per segment that the CFO trusts.

stages.narrative: On 30 September 2025 the day-ahead market moves to 15-minute blocks and the desk's Excel position model, built on hourly prices and monthly allocation exports, breaks down: valuation takes a morning, the dynamic-tariff segment cannot be separated from the fixed book, and a winter campaign sold more fixed contracts than the desk had hedged. The CFO asks how much the portfolio is really worth today and gets three different answers.

The portfolio manager reads Eneve's review of the 2025 Dutch market changes, hears from the supplier's billing team that their Supplier Suite vendor also offers sourcing and pricing modules, and meets a peer desk at a TenneT market-party session that runs positions per segment on the same platform. A demo shows allocated and forecast volumes per 15-minute block, hedges applied to coverage, and value per segment on one screen.

The desk compares extending the spreadsheet model, buying a generic energy trading and risk management system, and adopting the Trade and Portfolio Suite on the platform that already holds the contracts and allocation data. Decisive checks are the segment attribution of existing contracts, how PPAs and click contracts are represented, whether the price curves can feed the proposition builder, the audit trail the risk committee needs, and the per-portfolio subscription against the analyst hours it replaces.

For one quarter the desk runs the suite in parallel: segments are defined, the hedge book is loaded, and the daily position is compared with the spreadsheet. The differences turn out to be real: two PPAs valued on the wrong profile and a segment of dynamic contracts that had been counted as fixed. The CFO signs off when the settlement invoice reconciles to the suite's numbers within one percent.

The spreadsheet is retired. The desk starts the day with the 15-minute position per segment, the hedging strategy and limits live in the suite, alerts replace the Monday export, and the proposition team prices the spring campaign from the curves the desk maintains, with the coverage check built into the launch.

At renewal the desk adds the risk analytics module and the customer trading desk for its B2B book, the CFO uses the segment margin view in the monthly close, and the risk committee writes the suite's limit reports into its charter. Leaving would mean rebuilding the segment history and the link to billing and allocation that now make the position trustworthy.

customerJourneyStories.name: Adopting cost-plus pricing and deal structuring for the B2B book
customerJourneyStories.summary: A portfolio and origination manager at the Benelux desk of an international BRP already running positions on the platform adopts the cost-plus pricing and deal structuring capabilities after a badly priced industrial click contract, and turns B2B quoting into a same-day process with tracked margin.

stages.narrative: An industrial customer clicks a full delivery year at a price the desk had quoted from a stale curve; the hedge is executed at a loss and the deal's margin is negative before the first delivery. The head of origination wants every quote built from the live curves and every click to hit the hedge book the same hour.

During the quarterly account review the platform's customer success manager shows the pricing and customer trading modules the desk licenses but has not switched on: cost-plus pricing from the maintained curves, contract structuring with click rules and tolerance bands, and the customer trading desk that records clicks against the position. A supplier reference describes pricing multi-site tenders in an afternoon.

The desk and the risk manager check whether the cost-plus model covers profile, imbalance and guarantee-of-origin components the way their internal policy prescribes, how click limits and windows are enforced, whether the audit trail of a quote would satisfy the trade-surveillance review, and what integration with the group's trading system is needed. Two recent tenders are re-priced in the tool and compared with the original quotes.

For two months all new B2B tenders are priced through the cost-plus model and one industrial framework contract is migrated to the customer trading desk. Quotes go out the same day, the industrial customer's clicks appear in the hedge book within the hour, and the risk manager sees the reserved volume per structured deal for the first time.

The pricing policy per segment is maintained in the suite, sales and the desk share the quote pipeline, and realised margin per deal is reviewed monthly against what was priced. Producers' PPAs are structured with the same tool and their output feeds the position directly.

The desk expands the licence to the group's Belgian portfolio when the platform's Belgian market adapters arrive, and asks for a pricing API so brokers can request indicative quotes directly. The margin discipline the tool created has become part of how the desk is measured.

customers.name: BRP and Balancing Operator
customers.description: Runs the daily balance-responsibility cycle for an electricity and gas portfolio: day-ahead, intraday and ex-post forecasting per EAN type, E-programme nominations and re-nominations to TenneT and gas nominations to the gas TSO, intraday steering through the ETPA trading cycle and flexible assets, and the allocation, reconciliation, imbalance settlement and BRP compliance reporting that follow under Allocation 2.0. Typical employer: the BRP desk of an international trader such as Axpo, TotalEnergies or Vattenfall, a gas shipper such as EBN, the in-house BRP of a Dutch supplier, or Eneve's own BRP as a Service desk that carries balance responsibility for suppliers with portfolios from 40 GWh. Works in 15-minute programme time units with a 24-hour operations rota and a gate closure that never moves.
careAbout: A day-ahead forecast per EAN type, including solar, wind, batteries and telemetry connections, that is good enough that the E-programme is right before the intraday desk has to fix it
Every nomination and re-nomination to TenneT and the gas TSO submitted before gate closure, with a confirmed receipt and an alert when an interface fails, day and night
An intraday position per 15-minute block that is near real time, so the desk decides to trade on ETPA or steer assets while it still matters
Allocation and reconciliation volumes from the TenneT MMC-Hub that match nominations and meter data, with rejections and deviations handled the same day rather than in the next reconciliation run
An imbalance settlement invoice from TenneT that can be verified line by line against the portfolio's own data and passed on to the right segment or customer
Imbalance cost per MWh that falls year on year and can be shown to management and to the suppliers the desk serves
winsThem: Forecasting, nomination and re-nomination for electricity and gas as one automated cycle with the operator supervising exceptions, instead of scripts and spreadsheets stitched together by whoever is on shift
An ETPA intraday trading cycle run as a guaranteed process with position, price and volume limits, so the desk closes the gap in the position without a trader watching a screen all night
Steering signals to batteries, solar parks and flexible customer assets from the same position the trades are made on, with the effect visible in the next 15-minute block

Allocation 2.0 reconciliation, MMC-Hub exchange and imbalance settlement verification handled in the same data model as the nominations, so a dispute is an exception report rather than a research project
The option to outsource the whole cycle as BRP as a Service with tiered per-MWh pricing, keeping the portfolio visibility while the operational risk moves to a specialist desk
theirFear: A missed gate closure on a windy Sunday because the nomination interface failed silently and nobody on shift saw it, leaving a full day of imbalance at prices that wipe out a month of margin
A reconciliation run that reveals the portfolio was allocated volumes it never nominated because a switch batch had not reached the BRP's register, months after the fact
A steering signal that discharges a customer's battery at the wrong moment and turns a hedge into an imbalance position while the customer's site loses power quality

jobsToBeDone.name: Forecast and nominate the portfolio accurately and on time
jobsToBeDone.whatItIs: Every day, for every EAN type in the portfolio, produce the day-ahead forecast, match it to the procured position, build and submit the E-programme to TenneT and the gas nominations to the gas TSO before gate closure, update the forecast intraday and re-nominate when the position changes, and review ex post how good the forecast was.
jobsToBeDone.outcome: Nominations reflect the best available forecast and the procured volumes, arrive before every gate closure with a confirmed receipt, and are corrected intraday as the position changes, so the imbalance the desk has to settle is the residual that could not be known, not the result of a missed deadline or a stale forecast.

jobsToBeDone.name: Steer intraday to minimise imbalance cost
jobsToBeDone.whatItIs: Within the day, watch the portfolio position per 15-minute block against the E-programme, decide whether to close deviations by trading on ETPA or by steering batteries, solar parks and flexible customer assets, execute those actions as a guaranteed cycle, and learn from the imbalance result of every block.
jobsToBeDone.outcome: Deviations from the programme are closed at the cheapest available action before the block is settled, steering never harms a customer's site, and the imbalance cost per MWh falls towards the portfolio's residual, unavoidable level.

steps.step: Watch the near real-time position per 15-minute block
steps.description: Follow the position of the portfolio per block from telemetry, estimated small-consumer volumes and asset schedules, compared with the nominated programme and with the expected imbalance price direction published by TenneT.

customerJourneyStories.name: A supplier outsources balance responsibility to BRP as a Service
customerJourneyStories.summary: The balancing operator of a growing renewable supplier, whose in-house BRP setup could not keep up with Allocation 2.0 reconciliation, the 15-minute day-ahead market and rising imbalance prices, moves the portfolio to BRP as a Service and keeps the visibility while the operational risk moves to a specialist desk.

stages.narrative: In the first quarter of 2025 the reconciliation runs under Allocation 2.0 tranche 3 produce corrections the supplier's two-person BRP team cannot explain, imbalance costs on windy weekends have doubled with the portfolio's solar and wind share, and the 15-minute day-ahead change in September is approaching with a forecasting script that only knows hours. The director asks whether the company should still carry balance responsibility itself.

The operator finds Eneve's BRP as a Service page and the March 2025 announcement of the collaboration with Pure Energie, hears the managed-BRP proposition described at a TenneT market-party day, and asks the supplier's billing colleagues, who already run on the platform, for an introduction. A call with the operations desk explains the guaranteed forecasting, nomination and ETPA cycle and the claim of up to 53% lower imbalance cost.

The supplier compares hiring two more operators and rebuilding the tooling, joining another BRP's portfolio, and BRP as a Service. Decisive checks are the 40 GWh minimum portfolio and the tiered per-MWh pricing against the current imbalance and staff cost, how the supplier keeps its own position and cost visibility per segment, who is liable for a missed nomination, whether batteries and BSP assets are covered, and a reference call with a comparable supplier.

For one month the service runs in shadow mode: the desk forecasts and builds nominations for the supplier's portfolio next to the in-house team, and both results are compared with allocation per block. The shadow forecast is better for every EAN type, and a re-nomination the in-house team missed on a holiday would have cost more than a month of service fees.

Balance responsibility is transferred at the start of a month. The operator's role shifts to supervising the daily reports, the 15-minute financial insight per segment and the reconciliation results, and to feeding the desk with campaign volumes and new producer connections. The intraday cycle runs at night without anyone at the supplier awake.

After the first year the imbalance cost per MWh has fallen well below the in-house level, the supplier adds its first battery customers to the steered portfolio, and the operator spends the freed hours on the supplier's producer PPAs instead of on night shifts. Taking the role back would mean rebuilding a 24-hour desk and the tooling the service made unnecessary.

customerJourneyStories.name: A gas shipper adopts the Balancing and Shipping Suite for nominations and trading
customerJourneyStories.summary: The shipping operator of a gas producer and shipper, whose nomination and position management ran on a legacy in-house tool, adopts the Balancing and Shipping Suite for gas trading and shipping and ends up with automated nominations, verified settlements and a desk that can add electricity later.

stages.narrative: The shipper's in-house nomination tool, maintained by one retiring developer, fails a gas TSO interface change and a day of nominations has to be entered by hand. The board wants shipping and trading operations on a supported platform before the next gas year.

The operator knows the EBASE name from years of BRP market messages and finds that Energy21 has become Eneve, that EBN signed a gas trading and shipping agreement with it on 10 September 2024, and that the Balancing and Shipping Suite covers automated nominations and position management for both gas and electricity. A visit to the operations desk in Utrecht shows the nomination cycle and the settlement verification live.

The shipper evaluates the suite against a European gas trading system and a rebuild of the in-house tool. The checks that matter are the certified gas TSO interfaces and their monitoring, the handling of hourly nominations and re-nominations, how the suite verifies allocation and settlement against the shipper's own measurements, the security and continuity documentation for the auditors, and the option to add electricity balance responsibility later on the same platform.

A three-month pilot runs the nominations for one portion of the portfolio through the suite in parallel with the legacy tool, with the legacy tool remaining the system of record. The pilot delivers every nomination before gate closure, catches two settlement lines the shipper would have paid without question, and proves the interface monitoring during a planned TSO maintenance window.

The full portfolio moves at the start of the gas year. Nominations, position management and settlement verification run as one cycle, the operator works from exception lists instead of screens, and the trading desk sees the shipped position next to its trades. The legacy tool is switched off after two clean months.

At renewal the shipper extends the contract to include electricity nominations for its power assets and asks the desk for regulatory reporting from the same data. The suite is now the system the auditors and the TSO relationship depend on.

At an industrial energy users' association meeting the energy manager hears a peer from a site utility company describe clicking tranches from a tablet.

The energy manager and the procurement director compare staying with phone clicks, engaging a broker, and using the supplier's trading desk. They check the click limits and four-eyes approval, whether the framework contract terms are represented correctly, how the site's own measurements can be reconciled with the invoice breakdown, the audit trail for the internal auditors, and whether a second supplier's platform would lock them in.

For one quarter one site runs on the trading desk while the others stay on the phone. The manager executes three clicks with confirmation in minutes, submits the site's forecast from the production plan, and reconciles the quarterly invoice per connection without a query for the first time.

All sites move to the desk at the framework renewal. Price alerts arrive on the plant floor, the site controllers get their own read-only access to consumption and invoices, and the forecast per site is updated whenever a maintenance stop is planned. The CFO receives a monthly view of clicked prices against the market.

The group renews the framework contract with the supplier for another three years, partly because the trading desk has become the group's procurement tool, and asks the supplier about steering its new battery. Moving to another supplier would mean losing the click history, forecasts and reconciled invoices per site.

customerJourneyStories.name: Monetising a site battery and CHP through the supplier's BRP
customerJourneyStories.summary: The utility manager of an industrial site with a new battery and an existing CHP unit adopts the flexible-asset steering offered through the supplier's platform and BRP, after being courted by aggregators, and ends up with flex revenue on the same invoice as supply and constraints the site controls.

stages.narrative: The site's new 10 MW battery sits mostly idle after commissioning, the CHP unit is run on a fixed schedule regardless of the market, and three aggregators have offered to take over the assets with contracts the site's engineers do not trust. The board wants the assets to earn money without a single production incident.

The supplier, whose BRP already nominates the site, explains that its balancing platform steers batteries, CHP and curtailable load within customer constraints and that the value is settled on the supply invoice. The utility manager reads about the November 2025 aFRR changes with 0.1 MW setpoints and 4-hour capacity auctions and asks how the site's assets could qualify.

The site compares the aggregator offers with steering through the supplier's BRP. The engineers test the constraint model, the override and the emergency stop; the controller compares the revenue share and the settlement transparency; the energy manager checks the imbalance, intraday and aFRR use cases and whether the site keeps its own view of every activation. A reference call with another steered industrial site settles the engineers' doubts.

A three-month pilot steers the battery only, within conservative state-of-charge limits and outside production-critical hours. Every activation is visible per block, the constraints hold during a test override, and the pilot revenue appears on the next invoice with a breakdown per activation.

The CHP unit and a curtailable process are added to the agreement, the constraints are widened after the engineers see the response data, and the site's utility team checks the activation report every morning. The aFRR product is added when the assets are prequalified.

The site renews the flexibility agreement together with the supply contract, adds a second battery sized on the activation data, and the group's other sites ask for the same constraint model. The aggregators stop calling once the site's flex revenue and its supply are settled on one invoice.

stages.narrative: The Allocation 2.0 tranche 3 reconciliation and the 15-minute day-ahead market land in the same year, each requiring a change project in three different systems, while the annual settlement run produces a correction rate the auditors flag. The COO concludes that the company is paying five vendors and a BRP to keep pieces of one process alive and that the next market change will break it.

The June 2025 announcement that Energy21, Ecedo, Jules and Gridhub have become Eneve explains that the supplier's heritage billing package and its BRP's balancing platform now belong to one company with a consolidation roadmap. At an industry meeting the director of a comparable supplier describes running onboarding, billing, the customer portal and BRP as a Service on the same data model, and the reference logos on the vendor site are companies the COO competes with.

The vendor loads one of the supplier's brands from a heritage export and demonstrates a switch through EDSN, a billing run with guarantees of origin and split invoicing, a customer dispute in the portal and the resulting allocation and settlement view. The CFO checks the cost to serve business case against the licence, hosting and specialist cost of the heritage stack; the compliance officer reviews the market-change delivery record for 2025; two reference calls and a written migration plan with parallel run and support-until-decommission terms settle the decision.

The trial is a parallel run on the smallest brand of 40,000 connections: customers, connections, contracts, meter histories and open invoices are migrated, the next two billing runs and one month of allocation and settlement run in both systems, and invoices and volumes are compared line by line. Three mapping issues in guarantees-of-origin lines are fixed within a week and the controller signs off the first month close from the platform.

Within a year every brand and connection runs on the platform, the customer portal carries each brand, the third-party BRP contract is replaced by BRP as a Service, and the weekly operations meeting runs from the 15-minute margin dashboard. Two heritage contracts are terminated ahead of schedule and the proposition team launches a dynamic EV tariff in five weeks without an IT ticket.

Renewal is decided on numbers: cost to serve per connection is down by a third, the correction rate is below one percent and the 2026 market changes shipped without a project. The COO joins the customer advisory board, adds the Trade & Portfolio suite for the B2B desk and gives the reference call to the next supplier considering consolidation.

stages.narrative: A volatile quarter produces imbalance cost twice the budget, the senior balancing specialist resigns and the 15-minute day-ahead market and the November 2025 aFRR changes are weeks away. The CFO decides that a two-person desk with a spreadsheet forecasting model is an uninsured risk, not a capability.

A trader at a partner company mentions that its portfolio is balanced by a managed BRP with a guaranteed cycle; the vendor's BRP as a Service page describes day-ahead, intraday and ex-post forecasting, TenneT nominations and re-nominations, ETPA intraday trading and up to 53% reduction in imbalance costs for portfolios from 40 GWh. The CFO recognises the vendor as the company behind the balancing platform its supplier already uses.

The vendor runs a back-test on twelve months of the portfolio's allocation data and shows what the guaranteed cycle would have cost and saved, per segment and per 15 minutes. The CFO compares tiered MWh pricing against the desk's fully loaded cost and the imbalance overrun, legal reviews the contract for balance responsibility and liability, and the risk committee checks that positions remain visible to the company in near real time. A reference from a wind and solar producer settles it.

The trial covers the solar production part of the portfolio for one quarter: forecasts, nominations and intraday steering run under the managed service while the desk keeps the rest, and imbalance cost per MWh is compared segment by segment every week. The first month shows the forecast error halving on sunny days and the CFO extends the trial to the supply portfolio.

Within six months the whole portfolio, including gas, is nominated and steered under BRP as a Service; the former desk specialists move into portfolio and pricing work; the 15-minute financial insight per segment becomes part of the monthly board pack and the basis for hedging decisions.

The service renews on a three-year term because imbalance cost per MWh is below the back-test, the aFRR and 15-minute market changes landed without the company noticing, and the vendor's quarterly review has become the CFO's window on the market. The company adds the Trade & Portfolio suite and asks the vendor to scope balance responsibility for its planned Belgian portfolio.

customerJourneyStories.name: A Dutch founder launches a dynamic-tariff supplier in nine months
customerJourneyStories.summary: The founder of a start-up that wants to sell 15-minute dynamic and EV tariffs to prosumers adopts the platform and its expertise services: triggered by the 15-minute day-ahead market and the net-metering phase-out, discovering the vendor through an ACM licence list and an investor, evaluating the market-entry scan and BRP as a Service against building a team, trialling with the five-week scan and a licensing engagement, and staying because the first customers went live within months and the platform kept pace with growth.

stages.narrative: The move of the Dutch day-ahead market to 15-minute blocks and the announced 2027 phase-out of net metering convince the founder that prosumers with solar, batteries and EVs will need a supplier that prices per quarter hour. The seed round is closed on the promise of first customers within a year, and the founder has no licence, no BRP and no billing system.

Scanning the ACM list of licensed suppliers, the founder notices that several recent entrants run on the same platform; an investor who backed one of them names the vendor and its market-entry scan. The vendor's site describes five workstreams in five weeks, ACM licensing support of 8 to 14 weeks and the warning that most entrants underestimate the licensing ramp by six months or more, which matches what the founder has heard.

The founder compares the scan plus platform plus BRP as a Service route against hiring a balancing specialist, a billing developer and a market-communication consultant. A reference call with an entrant that went live the year before, a sample scan report, the tiered MWh pricing from 40 GWh and the fact that the platform's connectors are already certified with EDSN settle it; the board approves the scan as the first spend.

The five-week scan delivers the regulatory checklist, the competitive overview of dynamic-tariff suppliers, an operating model with BRP as a Service and outsourced payment collection, a commercial blueprint with three launch propositions and a roadmap. The go decision follows, and the licensing engagement starts with a complete ACM submission in the sixth week.

While the ACM processes the application, the launch team configures the propositions, onboarding, billing and the branded app, passes the EDSN certification tests on the platform's connectors and trains in the academy. The licence arrives in week twelve; the first two hundred customers are switched, billed and balanced under the managed BRP in month nine.

A year after go-live the supplier has 20,000 connections, a correction rate below two percent and imbalance cost in line with the back-test; the platform subscription and MWh pricing scale with the base rather than with headcount. The founder commissions a Belgian market-entry scan on the same platform.

customerJourneyStories.name: A Northern-European utility opens a Spanish retail business
customerJourneyStories.summary: The expansion lead of a Dutch utility that wants to sell electricity to SMEs in Spain adopts the Iberian supplier platform and licensing services: triggered by a board mandate to grow outside the home market, discovering the vendor's Spanish capability through the Nemon acquisition, evaluating the CNMC timeline and the SIPS and ATR market communication against a local acquisition, trialling with a dual-market scan, and staying because one platform now runs both countries.

stages.narrative: The board asks for a second country within two years and Spain's SME segment, where about a hundred suppliers compete and solar production is growing, comes out top of the internal screening. The expansion lead knows the Dutch platform well but nothing about CNMC registration, SIPS, ATR access or OMIE.

The March 2026 news that the utility's Dutch platform vendor has acquired Nemon, with about a hundred supplier customers in Spain and Portugal, reaches the expansion lead through the vendor's account manager and an industry newsletter. The vendor's dual-market entry scan and the 16 to 20 week combined licensing timeline are exactly the questions on the expansion lead's desk.

The expansion lead compares a greenfield entry on the Iberian platform with buying a small Spanish supplier and its systems. The vendor presents Nemon's Trade Energy, CRM and SIPS modules with references from Spanish suppliers, a CNMC registration plan of 12 to 20 weeks and a cross-border operating model in which the Dutch portfolio desk prices the Spanish book. Legal checks the guarantees, finance the setup cost per market, and the group CIO the fact that both countries will report into one data model.

The trial is the five-week dual-market scan with the Spanish regulatory workstream, a competitive overview of the SME segment, the operating model and a blueprint of three cost-plus propositions. The scan surfaces a guarantee requirement the utility had not budgeted and a distributor switching-file process that needs SIPS access from week one; both go into the plan before the go decision.

The CNMC registration is granted in week sixteen; the Spanish operation goes live on the Iberian platform with OMIE and REE connections, SIPS switching and a Spanish-language portal, while Dutch pricing and risk teams see the Spanish positions in the same dashboards. The first thousand SME sites are supplied within a year.

The Spanish business renews and expands to Portugal on the same platform because setup cost per market came in under budget and the two-country operation needs no second back office. The expansion lead's next request is a German market-entry scan on the same operating model.

customers.name: Household or Business Energy Customer
customers.description: A household, small business or multi-site SME supplied by one of the platform's supplier tenants in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain or Portugal: one of the 7 million households and 3 million business customers served by Dutch supplier clients, or a Spanish SME supplied through a Nemon-based supplier. Signs up or switches through a comparison site, a sales channel or the supplier's own site, moves house, receives monthly advances and an annual settlement or monthly actual-usage bills, and increasingly has solar panels, a heat pump, an EV or a home battery on a dynamic or time-of-use contract. Uses the supplier's white-label portal and app for free to see invoices and consumption, submit meter readings, change tariff, advance or payment method, raise a dispute or a service request, and expects the bill to be right and the answer to be available without calling. Judges the supplier, and indirectly the platform, on bill accuracy, ease of self-service and how fast a switch, move-in or dispute is handled.

Switching or moving in on the requested date without a rejected switch, a double bill or a gap in supply
Doing things themselves in the app at any hour: readings, tariff and advance changes, payment method, moving, a question, a complaint
Fair treatment when money is tight: a payment plan, a warning before dunning, no disconnection without contact
Trust that the supplier follows the rules on tariffs, contract terms, notice periods and price changes
winsThem: An app that shows consumption, cost and the next invoice on the same numbers the supplier bills from, so what the customer sees is what they pay

Meter readings, tariff changes and payment arrangements that take two minutes and need no call or letter
A dispute that can be raised in the app with the invoice attached and answered by someone who sees the same data
Propositions that fit the household: dynamic pricing, EV charging tariffs, battery and solar bundles offered when they make sense
theirFear: An annual settlement demanding hundreds of euros because advances were set on an estimate nobody corrected

customerJourneyStories.name: A household switches to a dynamic contract and stays for the app
customerJourneyStories.summary: A family with solar panels and a new EV in Utrecht switches to a supplier on the platform for a dynamic quarter-hour tariff and adopts the supplier's white-label app: triggered by an annual settlement shock and the coming net-metering phase-out, discovering the supplier through a comparison site and a neighbour's app, evaluating on transparent quarter-hour pricing and reviews, trialling with the switch and the first month of consumption insight, and staying because the app makes the bill understandable.

stages.narrative: The annual settlement from the current supplier asks for EUR 480 because the advance was set before the EV arrived, and a news item explains that net metering for solar will end in 2027. The family wants a contract where the EV charges when electricity is cheap and the solar feed-in is visible, and a supplier whose bill they can check.

A comparison site lists several dynamic-tariff suppliers; a neighbour shows the app of one of them with quarter-hour prices, charging cost per session and feed-in per day. The family recognises the supplier from an EV forum where members praise the fact that the app shows the same numbers as the invoice.

The family compares the dynamic tariff against a fixed contract with an EV add-on, reads the terms on price components, notice period and how the advance is set, checks reviews on switching problems and consumer-organisation ratings, and confirms that the app supports readings, disputes and payment changes. The transparent breakdown and the fact that the switch date is guaranteed decide it.

The sign-up takes five minutes; the switch is confirmed for the first of the month and the app is active before supply starts. In the first month the family checks daily consumption, sets the EV to charge in the cheap night hours and sees the projected annual cost fall; the first invoice matches what the app predicted to the euro.

The app becomes a weekly habit: the family watches feed-in in summer, adjusts the advance before winter, submits a reading when the smart meter has a gap and raises one dispute about a grid-charge line that is answered with the reading in two days. No call is ever made.

When a competitor offers a cheaper fixed contract the family stays: the annual settlement is a small refund, the bill is understandable and the supplier has just offered a battery bundle in the app for the post-net-metering years. They recommend the supplier on the EV forum that brought them.

customerJourneyStories.name: A small business with three sites moves onto the supplier's portal
customerJourneyStories.summary: The owner of a bakery with three shops in Rotterdam, supplied under one business contract, adopts the supplier's business portal: triggered by three separate paper invoices a month and a dispute nobody could trace, discovering the portal through the supplier's account manager and an invoice footer, evaluating on split invoicing and per-site insight, trialling with one site's history, and staying because the accountant now downloads everything and the bill is right.

stages.narrative: Every month three paper invoices arrive for three shops, one of them regularly on an estimated reading, and a disputed invoice from the spring has gone back and forth by e-mail for eight weeks while the direct debit kept running. The owner wants one place to see what each shop uses and pays.

The supplier's account manager mentions during the contract renewal that the business portal shows all sites, invoices and readings in one login and that the supplier moved to a new platform last year; the invoice footer and a renewal e-mail carry the same invitation. The owner's accountant has seen the portal at another client.

The owner looks at whether the portal shows consumption per shop, whether invoices can be split per site and downloaded for the accountant, whether readings can be submitted with a photo when a meter is not read remotely, and whether a dispute can be raised on a specific invoice. A short demo by the account manager and the supplier's promise that the portal data is the billing data settle it.

The owner activates the portal, adds the accountant as a user and starts with one shop: twelve months of readings and invoices are there, the estimated reading is replaced by a submitted one with a photo and a corrected invoice appears within a week. The spring dispute is re-raised in the portal and closed in four days.

All three shops are managed in the portal, invoices are split per site and pulled by the accountant monthly, the advance for the busiest shop is raised before the winter and the owner checks weekly consumption after installing a new oven. Contact with the supplier drops to one question a year.

At the next renewal the owner accepts the supplier's offer with a rooftop solar feed-in proposition for the largest shop, chosen in the portal, rather than tendering the contract. Bill accuracy and the accountant's time saved outweigh the small price difference a competitor offers.
